accroche: Eight fake patients get themselves admitted to psychiatric hospitals in 1973: the study has since proved largely unverifiable.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1973, David Rosenhan, a psychologist at Stanford, and seven other volunteers present themselves at twelve American psychiatric hospitals. Each claims to hear voices saying words like “hollow,” “empty,” “thud.” All are admitted. Seven receive a diagnosis of schizophrenia, the last one that of manic-depressive psychosis. Their stays last from seven to fifty-two days, and none is ever identified as a fake patient by the care staff.

## The Mechanism

Rosenhan publishes these results in *Science* under the title “On Being Sane in Insane Places.” His argument: psychiatric diagnosis depends more on the context one is in than on the behavior actually observed. The hospital itself, he writes, imposes an environment where the meaning of behavior is easily misunderstood, and whose effects on patients (powerlessness, depersonalization, segregation, humiliation, self-labeling) seem to him countertherapeutic. Yet he does not blame the staff: the pseudo-patients perceived them as attentive, committed, and very intelligent, and he attributes the failings to the environment rather than to individuals.

In a second phase, Rosenhan warns a hospital that fake patients will present themselves in the coming months. Of 193 new patients evaluated, the staff judge 41 to be impostors, when Rosenhan has sent none. For him, the demonstration is made in both directions: the system fails to detect the fakers who are present, and it invents them in their absence.

The article has an immense impact. It is often credited with having weighed in the 1980 overhaul of the diagnostic criteria of the DSM-III, made more operational. Robert Spitzer criticizes the study as early as 1975, citing Seymour Kety's objection: psychiatrists cannot be expected to start from the assumption that a patient is faking.

## What This Shifts

In 2019, the journalist Susannah Cahalan publishes *The Great Pretender*, an investigation into the study and its author. She manages to identify only two of the eight announced pseudo-patients, Rosenhan himself among them, and wonders whether the other six existed. In 2023, the historian Andrew Scull calls the study, in *History of Psychiatry*, “a successful scientific fraud.”

The irony closes in on itself. A study that accused psychiatry of mistaking a label for a verified fact rests, fifty years later, on data whose reliability is called into question.

carte.punch: The study that changed American psychiatry does not withstand its own investigation.
carte.idee: In 1973, eight fake patients get themselves admitted to psychiatric hospitals without ever being detected. The study weighs in the overhaul of American diagnostic criteria: before a 2019 investigation manages to identify only two of the eight announced participants.

quiz.question: What is Rosenhan's central argument in “On Being Sane in Insane Places”?
choix: That American psychiatric hospitals lacked qualified staff in 1973
That psychiatric diagnosis depends more on the admission context than on the behavior actually observed
That schizophrenia should no longer be considered a valid diagnosis
That patients who fake symptoms should be criminally prosecuted for fraud
quiz.explication: Rosenhan argues that the label applied at admission, “schizophrenic,” leads the staff to reinterpret all later behavior as a symptom, to the point that none of the eight fake patients is detected. The study is not about the validity of schizophrenia as a disorder, nor about hospital staffing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens when Rosenhan warns a hospital that fake patients will present themselves there?
choix: The staff immediately detect the eleven fake patients actually sent
The hospital refuses to admit any new patient for several months
Of 193 real patients evaluated, 41 are judged impostors by at least one staff member, when Rosenhan has sent none
All admitted patients are diagnosed as sane as a precaution
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rosenhan sends no fake patients, but of 193 real patients evaluated, the staff suspect 41 of being impostors, proof in his view that the system invents fakers in their absence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Susannah Cahalan's 2019 investigation find about the eight fake patients announced by Rosenhan?
choix: It confirmed the documented identity of the eight original participants
It could identify only two of the eight announced pseudo-patients, Rosenhan himself among them
It found the twelve hospitals but none of the participants
It proved that the study actually involved sixteen fake patients
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Susannah Cahalan, in her 2019 investigation, manages to identify only two of the eight pseudo-patients announced by Rosenhan, Rosenhan himself included, which casts doubt on the existence of the other six.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What diagnoses do Rosenhan's eight fake patients receive at admission?
choix: No diagnosis is made, for lack of sufficient symptoms
Bipolar disorder for all eight participants
A personality disorder for seven of them, and an anxiety disorder for the last
Schizophrenia for seven of them, and manic-depressive psychosis for the last
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Seven of the eight fake patients receive a diagnosis of schizophrenia at admission, and the last that of manic-depressive psychosis, despite identical behavior once admitted.
